prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which a magic-wavelength lattice traps many atoms free of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors, and for its demonstration and development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I move from B054 to B042, and I want the reason recorded as scientific and not as counting. Reading all eight round-1 files, the clock case survives the tests I would apply to my own first choice. The magic-wavelength condition is a clean, quantitative idea that can be checked against level structure: choose the trapping wavelength so that the differential light shift of the two clock states vanishes, and a large ensemble is held without Doppler or recoil shifts. This is closely related to how I think about a calculation that predicts a spectrum and is then confirmed by measurement. Independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) have rebuilt the clocks and compared them at the 1e-18 level, and the uncertainty budgets are understood. That is the independent confirmation I asked of B054 and that B054 has not yet delivered for its interpretation. The credit is also compact: Katori for the lattice concept and first demonstrations, Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier. Two names fit the three-person limit with room to spare, and no part of the physics requires a second prize part.
statement.case_against: My own earlier ranking of B042 was seventh, and the reason has not vanished: I remain more comfortable with a discovery of new matter or new quantum behaviour than with a measurement achievement. Danielsson, Lindroth and Mehlig correctly note that gravity, constants and dark-matter results so far are null or prospective, so the case rests on a new measurement regime and not on a violated theory. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems cover adjacent ground, and a sceptic can call lattice clocks a successor step. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups cannot all be absorbed by two names. I judge these to be real but manageable by careful wording, and I cannot adjudicate the AMO priority record myself. B054 remains, in my view, the more novel physics, and I think it will be ripe within a few years.

responses.point: Danielsson calls the lattice clock an invention and a precision frontier, not yet a discovery about nature, and notes that no deviation from general relativity or the Standard Model has been found; he will reconsider B054 only if its central claim is robust against twist-angle disorder.
responses.response: I accept his condition on B042 as stated: the fundamental-physics payoff is prospective, and the citation should not claim otherwise. That is why my citation names the invention and the 1e-18 performance and leaves out any claim about new tests. On B054 I cannot give him a disorder-proof argument today. The correlated insulators and superconducting domes have been seen in many independent devices, but the sample dependence is real and the pairing mechanism is open, so I concede that waiting is defensible. I would only ask him to keep B054 on the list as the leading condensed-matter candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I accept a timing argument for B054, or think it undervalues how quickly the field was reproduced, and he weighs independent confirmation over several years heavily.
responses.response: I accept the timing argument for this year, with one qualification. Fast reproduction of the phenomena is real evidence, but it is not the same as a stable interpretation, and a prize citation has to say what was discovered. The clocks have years of cross-laboratory comparison behind a settled interpretation, and B054 does not yet. I do not think speed of confirmation is undervalued in principle, but it does not substitute for a mature account. I would also support his request that the committee record why Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups are not credited.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B007 on the stability of the Z2 classification over fifteen years, regards the 2016 prize as covering many-body and Chern-type topology, and admits that omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu is the weak point of his choice.
responses.response: I agree that B007 is better consolidated than B054, and the Z2 step is distinct from the 2016 lineage. My difficulty is the one he names: any three-name credit leaves a serious claim outside it, because the HgTe proposal and the three-dimensional work belong to people who cannot be added. The attribution for B042 is simpler. I would ask him whether he accepts that this decides it for a single-prize year, since he already lists B042 as his fallback. I keep B007 as my second alternative and would not oppose it later if the credit question could be resolved.

responses.point: Lindroth checked the clock case on its own terms, describes the magic-wavelength lattice as a discovery about making an atom a clean quantum system, and flags novelty against 2005 and 2012 and a possible third contributor as the open points.
responses.response: Her account of the magic-wavelength condition persuades me that this is a physical idea and not only an engineering refinement, which was my chief doubt. I rely on her and Kroll for the primary literature on a third name, because I cannot test it myself. If she finds a contributor with a real claim to the lattice concept itself, and not only to the accuracy record, I would want that weighed before the vote. Absent that evidence, I do not see a basis to depart from two names.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the ensemble lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize, and wants the citation to state why Katori's role as originator and Ye's role at the frontier justify the two names.
responses.response: I agree and have drawn my citation accordingly: it names the magic-wavelength lattice as the invention and the demonstration and development to 1e-18 as the second element, which gives Katori the concept and Ye the frontier. I would not let the pending redefinition of the second drive our decision, since it is a metrological decision and not a physical result. The disclosed link between Kroll and Hall's laboratory does not seem to me to call for recusal, since Ye's claim does not run through the comb.

uncertainties: Whether lattice-clock comparisons yield competitive bounds on constants, dark matter or gravity, or whether the physics payoff remains prospective; I cannot judge this independently.

Whether primary literature gives a third contributor a claim to the lattice concept itself, and whether Ye's credit rests on distinct inventions or mainly on accuracy records, which I defer to AMO colleagues on.
Whether my move to B042 undervalues the speed with which B054 has been confirmed, and whether the pairing mechanism will prove to be a limit on the citation or a reason to wait.
How the committee should record the reasons for excluding other lattice-clock groups.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize, which is not a conflict. My field overlap with moire and topological materials is scientific, not personal, and my change of preference was not influenced by any disclosed connection of other members.
